warmup.q: The payments app needs the number of different cards that paid at one shop today, about 2 million cards, updated every minute. Being within 1% of the truth is good enough. Which way of keeping track uses the least memory in Redis?
options: A set of card numbers (a collection that holds each one once), counted with SCARD
A HyperLogLog (a small summary of fixed size that estimates how many different items it has seen), read with PFCOUNT
A list with one card number per payment, counted with LLEN
A sorted set of card numbers, each stored with its payment time, counted with ZCARD
warmup.why: A HyperLogLog never takes more than about 12 KB, and its estimate is usually within 0.81% of the truth. A set is exact, but it stores every card number: on the lab server, 100,000 numbers took about 4.4 MB, so 2 million would take tens of megabytes for each shop, every day. A list counts payments, not different cards, so a regular who pays three times counts three times. A sorted set is exact too, and bigger than a set, because it stores a time next to each card. This lesson is about that trade: structures that answer one narrow question in a small, fixed amount of memory, some of them by giving up exactness.

sections.h: One bit per card: counting active cards with a bitmap
sections.html:
Let's start with an exact question. The payments app knows a million cards, and the shop owners want to know which of them made a payment today. Redis stores each piece of data under a name called its key, like the label on a drawer. After Core data types and their encodings, the answer we'd reach for is a set, a Redis type that holds each item once. Each payment runs SADD cards:active:day1 card:417, where card:417 is the card's id, the short name the app knows it by. Adding a card that's already in the set changes nothing.

It works, and it's big. On the lab server, a set of a million card ids took about 30 MB, and the app needs a new one every day.

Look at what the set stores: the id of every active card, as text. Now suppose every card already has a number from 0 to 999,999. Then the number can be a position in a row, and all we need at each position is a yes or a no. A computer stores a yes or a no in one bit, a single 0 or 1, and eight bits make a byte. So a million cards need a million bits, which is 125,000 bytes. That's about 240 times smaller than the set, and it stays the same size whether 10 cards paid today or all of them did.

That row of bits, one per card, is a bitmap. Redis has no separate type for it. It uses a string, its simplest type: a run of bytes kept under one key. Then it adds commands that treat those bytes as a row of bits:

  • SETBIT cards:active:day1 417 1 sets bit 417 to 1. If the string is too short, Redis first grows it with zero bits.
  • GETBIT reads one bit.
  • BITCOUNT counts the 1 bits, which is the number of active cards.
  • BITOP combines whole bitmaps bit by bit and writes the answer to a new key. BITOP AND over the last 7 days, then BITCOUNT, gives the cards that paid on every one of those days. OR gives the cards that paid on any of them.

Each of those is one command over 125 KB per day, with no loop in your code. Redis 8.2 added four more BITOP operations: DIFF, DIFF1, ANDOR and ONE. BITOP DIFF dest day1 day2 keeps the cards that paid on day 1 but not on day 2. Before 8.2, you combine NOT and AND to get the same answer.

The price is the numbering. A bit's position is the card's number, so the numbers must be small and dense: 0, 1, 2 and on, with no big gaps. A number that the app's database (the program that keeps its permanent records) hands out in order, 1, 2, 3, works. If cards have no such number, give each one. A long, scattered id, such as a 16-digit card number, would need a bitmap as long as the biggest id. Positions stop at 2^32 - 1, about 4.3 billion, so one bitmap can't grow past 512 MB.

There's one more trap. Setting a bit near the end of an empty key makes Redis create every byte before it, all at once. Redis runs every command on one thread, a single path of work that handles one command at a time (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands showed why). So while it creates those bytes, every other program that uses this Redis waits. Redis 8.12, still a test release in November 2026, adds compressed bitmaps, called roaring bitmaps, that store scattered positions in little space. Check its final release notes before you design around them.

A bitmap's size is set by its highest position, not by how many bits are on. Give it small, dense numbers.

A bitmap needs every card to have a small number. Next, we'll take a question where the cards don't: how many different cards paid at each shop.

try.title: Track active cards for two days
steps: From the labs folder, start Redis with docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d. Docker is a program that runs other programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this command starts Redis 8.10 in one. Then open redis-cli, Redis's own window for typing commands: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli.
Type the commands below one at a time. Cards 7 and 42 paid on day 1 (card 42 twice), and cards 42 and 99 on day 2. Before each BITCOUNT, predict the number.
STRLEN gives a string's length in bytes. Before the last one, predict the size of a bitmap whose highest card number is 999,999.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SETBIT cards:active:day1 7 1
SETBIT cards:active:day1 42 1
SETBIT cards:active:day1 42 1
BITCOUNT cards:active:day1
SETBIT cards:active:day2 42 1
SETBIT cards:active:day2 99 1
BITOP AND cards:active:both cards:active:day1 cards:active:day2
BITCOUNT cards:active:both
BITOP OR cards:active:either cards:active:day1 cards:active:day2
BITCOUNT cards:active:either
BITOP DIFF cards:active:only1 cards:active:day1 cards:active:day2
BITCOUNT cards:active:only1
STRLEN cards:active:day1
SETBIT cards:active:day3 999999 1
STRLEN cards:active:day3
TYPE cards:active:day3

try.expect: SETBIT answers with the bit's old value: (integer) 0 the first time for card 42, and (integer) 1 the second time. Day 1 counts 2 cards, not 3 payments. AND finds 1 card (42), OR finds 3 (7, 42 and 99), and DIFF finds 1 (card 7, which paid on day 1 only). BITOP itself answers with the length of the string it wrote, (integer) 13, because bit 99 lives in byte 12 and bytes are counted from 0. Day 1 is 6 bytes long, while day 3 is (integer) 125000 bytes for a single bit that's on. TYPE says string: a bitmap is an ordinary string.

sections.h: Counting different cards in 12 KB with a HyperLogLog
sections.html:
Now a harder question: how many different cards paid at each shop this hour? There are 20,000 shops, and here the card ids are long and scattered, so a bitmap is out. (Even with small numbers, a 125 KB bitmap for every shop and hour would add up to 60 GB a day.) A set for each shop and hour is exact, and expensive: on the lab server, 100,000 card ids took about 4.4 MB.

Let's try the simplest counter first: run INCR, which adds one to a number kept under a key, on every payment. It counts payments, not cards: a card that pays three times counts three times. To skip the repeats, you must remember which cards you've already seen, and that's the set again. An exact count of different things needs memory that grows with the count.

So let's give up a little exactness. Picture a fair where you want to know how many people came, without writing down a single name. You ask each visitor to flip a coin until it lands heads, and to tell you how many tails came first. You keep one number: the longest run of tails anyone has reported. A run of 10 tails turns up about once in 1,024 tries, so if your record is 10, about a thousand people have probably come.

In code, the coin flips come from a hash function, a function that turns any text into a number that looks random. The same text always gives the same number. Hash each card id to a 64-bit number and read its bits from the right. Half of all hashes end in a 1, a quarter end in 10, an eighth in 100. Count the zeros before the first 1 and add one: that's the hash's rank, 1, 2 and 3 in those examples. A rank of r turns up about once in 2^r different cards, so a record rank of 10 means roughly 2^10, about a thousand, different cards.

Here the fair picture breaks, in our favor. A visitor who flips again gets a new run. A card that pays again has the same hash and the same rank, so it can't push the record up. Repeats are free.

One record is a wild guess, though. A single lucky card with 20 zeros would make you believe in a million cards. The fix is many records, combined. Split the cards into groups by a few bits of their hash, and keep the highest rank in each group. Then combine the groups with a kind of average that stops one lucky group from pulling the answer too far. Redis uses the lowest 14 bits of the hash to pick one of 16,384 groups, called registers, and takes the rank from the other 50 bits. A rank is at most 51, which fits in 6 bits. So 16,384 registers of 6 bits take 12,288 bytes.

That structure is a HyperLogLog. It takes at most 12 KB, and its standard error is 0.81%. That means about two times in three, the estimate is within 0.81% of the truth, whether you've added a thousand cards or a billion. In exchange, it can't list the cards it has seen, and it can't say whether one card is among them. It only counts. A small HyperLogLog starts in a compact, sparse form of a few dozen bytes and switches to the full 12 KB as it fills. Redis stores it as a string whose first bytes are HYLL, so TYPE says string.

Three commands do the work. PFADD key card ... adds cards and answers 1 if any register changed. PFCOUNT key gives the estimate. PFMERGE dest key ... keeps the larger value of each register across several keys, which gives exactly the HyperLogLog of all their cards together, so 24 hourly counters merge into one for the day. PFCOUNT with several keys does the same merge on the fly. The PF honors Philippe Flajolet, who invented the method.

Counting is one kind of question. Next comes a question about places: which card readers are near a point on a map.

The standard error is 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of registers: 0.81%. A small HyperLogLog starts in a sparse form of a few dozen bytes and switches to this full form as it fills.

try.title: Count 100,000 cards two ways
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the first four commands on a tiny HyperLogLog. Predict what the second PFADD answers.

Run the EVAL. EVAL runs a small program inside Redis as one command, written in Lua, a little programming language that Redis understands. This one adds the same 100,000 card ids to a HyperLogLog and to a set.
Predict how far PFCOUNT lands from 100,000. Then compare the memory of the two keys: MEMORY USAGE says how many bytes a key takes, counting Redis's own bookkeeping for it.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
PFADD visitors:today card:1 card:2 card:3
PFADD visitors:today card:1
PFCOUNT visitors:today
STRLEN visitors:today
EVAL "for i = 1, 100000 do redis.call('PFADD', KEYS[1], 'card:' .. i) redis.call('SADD', KEYS[2], 'card:' .. i) end return 1" 2 hll:cards set:cards
PFCOUNT hll:cards
SCARD set:cards
STRLEN hll:cards
MEMORY USAGE hll:cards
MEMORY USAGE set:cards
GETRANGE hll:cards 0 3

try.expect: The second PFADD answers (integer) 0: card:1 changed no register. PFCOUNT says 3, and the sparse HyperLogLog is only 27 bytes. After the EVAL, PFCOUNT hll:cards says (integer) 101058, 1.06% too high, while SCARD says exactly 100000. The HyperLogLog is in its full form now: STRLEN says 12304 (12,288 bytes of registers plus a 16-byte header), and MEMORY USAGE 14364. The set takes 4361843 bytes, about 300 times more. GETRANGE shows that the string starts with "HYLL". Redis always hashes the same way, so you get the same estimate on every run.

sections.h: Finding nearby card readers: a geo index is a sorted set
sections.html:
Next question: which card readers are within 5 km of a point on the map? The code calls a card reader a terminal. The app knows where each of its 100,000 terminals stands, as a longitude and a latitude, the two numbers that pin down a place on Earth.

The simplest version works out the distance to every terminal on every search. For 50 terminals, that's fine. For 100,000, each search keeps Redis's one thread busy while it walks the whole list, and every other program waits its turn.

What we want is to store nearby points next to each other in one sorted order, so that a search reads a short stretch instead of everything. Redis already has a type that reads stretches fast: the sorted set from Core data types and their encodings. It keeps its members in order of a number called the score, and finds the start of any range of scores in a few steps. What it needs is a score that keeps neighbors close together.

Here's how to build one. Split the world down the middle by longitude: west of the line is 0, east is 1. Then split it by latitude: south is 0, north is 1. Halve each half again, and again, taking turns between a longitude bit and a latitude bit. Each split adds one bit to the name of the cell that a point falls in. After 52 bits, the cell is less than a meter across, and the 52-bit number that names it is a geohash. Two points in the same small cell share the first bits of their geohash, so their numbers are close.

That's all a Redis geo index is: a sorted set whose scores are 52-bit geohashes. Scores are doubles, the numbers with a decimal point that computers use, and a double holds any 52-bit whole number exactly, so nothing is lost.

GEOADD terminals 4.8932 52.3731 t-dam stores a point, longitude first. GEOSEARCH terminals FROMLONLAT 4.8952 52.3702 BYRADIUS 5 km ASC WITHDIST finds the cells that cover the circle: the center cell and its 8 neighbors. It reads those ranges of scores, drops the points outside the circle, and returns the rest nearest first, with their distances. GEODIST gives the distance between two members. TYPE terminals says zset, Redis's short name for a sorted set, and to delete a point you use the sorted set command ZREM.

Two limits matter. Distances come from the Haversine formula, which treats the Earth as a perfect ball, and the Redis docs put the worst error at 0.5%. That's fine for "the nearest cash machine", and wrong where an exact distance has legal or money consequences. And latitudes stop at about 85.05 degrees north and south, so the areas around the poles can't be stored.

In a payments app, geo fits a fraud rule, a check that spots payments that look like a stolen card at work. Picture a card that pays at a terminal in Utrecht 12 minutes after it paid in Amsterdam, two cities in the Netherlands. GEODIST gives the 35 km between the two terminals in one call. That's a trip at 175 km/h, and your rule decides whether that's suspicious.

So far, each structure has counted or located. The last question is a plain yes or no, asked on every payment, and Redis 8 comes with a structure built for it.

try.title: Find card readers near the Dam
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, add five made-up terminals with one GEOADD: four in Amsterdam and one in Utrecht. The Dam is Amsterdam's main square.
Search within 5 km of a point near the Dam. Predict which terminals come back, and in what order.
Run the rest. What type is the key, and what's the score of t-dam? Then try to add a point at latitude 89, near the North Pole.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
GEOADD terminals 4.9003 52.3789 t-centraal 4.8932 52.3731 t-dam 4.8723 52.3389 t-zuid 4.7634 52.3105 t-schiphol 5.1214 52.0907 t-utrecht
GEOSEARCH terminals FROMLONLAT 4.8952 52.3702 BYRADIUS 5 km ASC WITHDIST
GEODIST terminals t-dam t-utrecht km
TYPE terminals
ZSCORE terminals t-dam
GEOPOS terminals t-dam
GEOADD terminals 0 89 t-pole

try.expect: GEOSEARCH returns t-dam at "0.3499" km, t-centraal at "1.0277" and t-zuid at "3.8131", nearest first. Schiphol (the airport) and Utrecht are more than 5 km away. GEODIST says "35.0466" km to Utrecht. TYPE says zset, and ZSCORE terminals t-dam is "3665667493069480", the 52-bit geohash. GEOPOS gives back 4.8931995034217834 and 52.37309930577733, a few centimeters from what you stored, because the geohash keeps 26 bits for each of the two numbers. Latitude 89 fails with ERR invalid longitude,latitude pair 0.000000,89.000000.

sections.h: Is this card on the stolen list? Bloom filters and Redis 8's built-ins
sections.html:
On every payment, the fraud check asks one more question: is this card on the list of cards whose details were stolen? The list holds a million card fingerprints. A fingerprint is a hash of the card number, so the list never holds the number itself. Nearly every card we check is not on the list. What we need is a cheap "no" that is always right, and we can afford a slower exact check for the rare "maybe".

The simplest version is a row of bits and one hash function. To add a fingerprint, hash it to a position and set that bit. To check one, look at its bit. A 0 means it was never added. A 1 means maybe, because some other fingerprint may have set the same bit. With a million fingerprints in 10 million bits, about one bit in ten is set, so about one check in ten gets a false "maybe".

Now use several hash functions. Adding a fingerprint sets all their bits, and a check says "maybe" only if every one of those bits is 1. The false answers drop fast. For a million fingerprints and 0.1% false answers, you need about 14.4 million bits (1.8 MB) and 10 hash functions. That's a Bloom filter, the structure that the Storage track's lesson LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters uses to skip files that can't hold a key. Its "no" is always right. Its "yes" is wrong at about the rate you chose, and a wrong yes is called a false positive. You also can't remove an item, because clearing its bits could erase other items that share them.

Before Redis 8, a Bloom filter needed a module, an add-on program loaded into Redis. Redis 8.0 moved several modules into Redis itself: the Query Engine, JSON, time series and vector sets (for finding similar items, still in beta at the time). It also brought in five structures that trade exactness for memory: the Bloom filter, the Cuckoo filter, the Count-min sketch, Top-k and t-digest. The official Docker image, the ready-made package that Docker runs, loads them all, and MODULE LIST on the lab server shows search, ReJSON, bf, timeseries and vectorset. Everything in this section needs Redis 8.0 or later. Valkey, a free copy of Redis that split off from it in 2024, may offer a different set. So may the Redis services that cloud companies run for you, so check before you design around them.

BF.RESERVE breached:cards 0.001 1000000 sets up a filter for a million items at a 0.1% false positive rate, and on the lab server it took about 1.9 MB. BF.ADD adds a fingerprint, and BF.EXISTS checks one.

JSON is a common text format for nested records, such as {"amount":1250,"card":{"last4":"4242"}}. Redis can keep a JSON document under a key and read or change one part of it by its path: JSON.SET payment:44 $ '{...}', JSON.GET payment:44 $.card.bin, JSON.NUMINCRBY payment:44 $.amount 50. Use it when a record is nested and you change parts of it. A flat record stays a hash, the Redis type that keeps a small table of fields and values under one key.

The rest are worth knowing by name. Time series (TS.ADD, TS.RANGE) store numbers stamped with a time, and drop the old ones after a while. The Query Engine (FT.CREATE, FT.SEARCH) makes hashes and JSON documents searchable. The Count-min sketch and Top-k answer "how often?" and "which are the most frequent?", approximately. Redis 8.8 added an Array type, marked as a preview that may still change. None of them is needed for the rest of this track.

Every structure in this lesson has the same limit: it answers one narrow question, and some answer it only roughly. A HyperLogLog is wrong for "how many different cards did we charge" on a bill to a shop, because 0.81% of a million is about 8,000 cards. A Bloom filter is wrong as the only check for "is this card blocked". A false positive turns away an honest customer, and you can't take an item out once it's in. The opposite mistake is keeping a set of 50 million ids only to read its size once an hour.

Decide first whether the answer must be exact. Then pick the structure.

And every one of these keys stays in memory until something removes it. Memory runs out, so sooner or later Redis has to forget.

try.title: Check a stolen-card list and change one field of a JSON payment
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run MODULE LIST and find the five built-in modules.
Run the Bloom filter commands. Predict the two BF.EXISTS answers, and what a second BF.RESERVE on the same key does.

BF.RESERVE breached:cards 0.001 1000000
BF.ADD breached:cards fp:9f2c41d7
BF.EXISTS breached:cards fp:9f2c41d7
BF.EXISTS breached:cards fp:0b77e310

The filter takes (integer) 1977672 bytes, about 1.9 MB, set aside up front for a million items. The second BF.RESERVE fails with (error) ERR item exists, so create a filter once, when you set the app up. JSON.GET ... $.card.bin returns "[\"411111\"]", a JSON list, because a $ path could match many places in a document. JSON.NUMINCRBY returns "[1300]", and the last JSON.GET shows the whole document with "amount":1300.

opening:
Picture the café owner from the payments app, the program that records every card payment: which card paid, which shop, how much and when. Today she wants one new number on her screen: how many different cards paid at her café today. A regular who buys three coffees counts once.

The company keeps numbers like this in Redis, a program that holds data in a computer's memory and answers commands from other programs. The obvious answer is a list of every card that paid. It's exact, and tiny for one café. For 20,000 shops, every hour, it grows with every new card: 100,000 cards took about 4.4 MB.

It's easy to believe that a count needs a list, because exact feels safe.

In Core data types and their encodings, we saw that the way data is arranged in memory decides its cost. In this lesson, we'll meet four structures that each answer one narrow question in a small, fixed amount of memory, and measure what exactness some give up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner who wanted to know how many different cards paid today, and a list that grew with every card. A HyperLogLog answers in 12 KB, off by less than 1%. A bitmap, a geo index and a Bloom filter each answer their own narrow question the same way.

Open an app you use that shows a count, such as the views on a video. Ask whether it needs to be exact, or whether 1% either way would do.

Next, we'll see how Redis forgets keys, by deadline and by choice, and find out why a key whose time is up can still sit in memory.

compare.title: A Bloom filter in front of the stolen-card table, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BreachCheck.java
java.html: // once, at deploy time: a filter for 1,000,000 fingerprints at a 0.1% false positive rate redis.bfReserve("breached:cards", 0.001, 1_000_000); boolean maybeBreached(String fingerprint) { if (!redis.bfExists("breached:cards", fingerprint)) return false; // "no" is always right return breachDb.contains(fingerprint); // "yes" needs the exact check }

kotlin.title: BreachCheck.kt
kotlin.html: // once, at deploy time: a filter for 1,000,000 fingerprints at a 0.1% false positive rate redis.bfReserve("breached:cards", 0.001, 1_000_000) fun maybeBreached(fingerprint: String): Boolean = redis.bfExists("breached:cards", fingerprint) && // "no" is always right breachDb.contains(fingerprint) // "yes" needs the exact check

compare.note: Both versions use Jedis, the Java library this track uses to talk to Redis, and the calls are the same. Kotlin's && stops early in the same way that the Java return false spells out: the database is asked only when the filter says yes. bfReserve fails with ERR item exists if the key is already there, so call it once from a setup step, not every time the app starts. Jedis 8 has the Bloom, JSON and time series commands built in, so neither version needs to send a raw command.

worked.title: Count different cards per shop, by hour and by day

steps.say: The shop owners want "different cards this hour" and "different cards today" on their screen, kept up to date. On every successful payment, add the card's fingerprint to the shop's HyperLogLog for the current hour. The code calls a shop a merchant, so shop m-17 at 14:00 has the key cards:m-17:h14. EXPIRE tells Redis to delete a key after a number of seconds, so old hours clear themselves away (the next lesson, Expiry, eviction and memory, looks inside it).
steps.code: String hourKey = "cards:" + merchant + ":h" + hour; // cards:m-17:h14 redis.pfadd(hourKey, fingerprint); // one fingerprint per approved payment redis.expire(hourKey, 172_800); // keep two days of hours

alt.html: val hourKey = "cards:$merchant:h$hour" // cards:m-17:h14 redis.pfadd(hourKey, fingerprint) // one fingerprint per approved payment redis.expire(hourKey, 172_800) // keep two days of hours

steps.say: The hourly number is one PFCOUNT. For the day, don't add up the 24 hourly counts: a card that paid at 9:00 and again at 15:00 would count twice. Count all the hours together instead. PFCOUNT with several keys merges them on the fly, and PFMERGE stores the merged HyperLogLog if you want to reuse it for a week.
steps.code: long thisHour = redis.pfcount(hourKey); String[] hours = IntStream.range(0, 24).mapToObj(h -> "cards:" + merchant + ":h" + h).toArray(String[]::new); long today = redis.pfcount(hours); // the union of 24 HyperLogLogs redis.pfmerge("cards:" + merchant + ":day", hours); // or store the union for the week view

alt.html: val thisHour = redis.pfcount(hourKey) val hours = (0 until 24).map { "cards:$merchant:h$it" }.toTypedArray() val today = redis.pfcount(*hours) // the union of 24 HyperLogLogs redis.pfmerge("cards:$merchant:day", *hours) // or store the union for the week view

steps.say: Check the cost. A busy shop has 24 full hourly keys of about 12 KB each, under 300 KB a day, and a quiet one stays in the sparse form at a few hundred bytes. A set for each hour would grow with every new card. The answer is off by about 0.81%, which is fine on a screen and not fine on a bill.

One thing it can't do is forget a card. A refunded payment stays counted, because a HyperLogLog has no way to remove anything. If the shops need "different cards that kept their purchase", that's a different, exact question. Keep the HyperLogLog for the live screen, and work out the exact number from the payments table, the app's record of every payment.

lab.title: Build a HyperLogLog, then count active cards with bitmaps
steps: Start Docker, then run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Gradle is the tool that builds the labs' Java and Kotlin code and runs their tests. All 13 tests fail at first: seven in TinyHyperLogLogTest, which check a small model of a HyperLogLog and need no Docker, and six in CardActivityTest, which use a real Redis in a container that all the tests share.

In TinyHyperLogLog.java, write add. Its comment lists four steps: hash the item, take the lowest p bits as the register number, count the zeros at the right end of the other bits and add 1, and keep the larger of the old and new values. Return true only if the register changed.

Write merge: register by register, keep the larger value. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l04.TinyHyperLogLogTest'. One test checks that merging two counters gives exactly the registers of one counter that saw both sets of cards.
In CardActivity.kt, write markActive, wasActive and activeCount with setbit, getbit and bitcount. Each is one line.

Write activeOnAllDays and activeOnAnyDay: bitop into a temporary key under the class's key prefix, bitcount it, and delete it in a finally block, so it goes away even when something fails. Run all 13 tests.
hints: Register number: (int) (h & ((1 << p) - 1)). The other bits: (h >>> p) | (1L << (64 - p)). The extra 1 on top stops the count when all the other bits are zero. Rank: Long.numberOfTrailingZeros(rest) + 1.
Registers are bytes. Compare with rank <= registers[index], and cast when you store: registers[index] = (byte) rank.
Jedis's bitop takes BitOP.AND or BitOP.OR, then the key to write, then the keys to combine: redis.bitop(BitOP.AND, tmp, *days.map(::keyFor).toTypedArray()). A day with no key counts as all zeros.
Make the temporary key unique, for example with a UUID (a random id), so two callers combining days at the same moment don't overwrite each other's result.

drill.title: Write HyperLogLog's add from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. You have p, a byte[] registers of size 2^p and a hash64(String) function. Write boolean add(String element) so that it updates the right register the way Redis does and returns whether anything changed. Then compare with the answer. Which bits pick the register, and why is there an extra 1 bit on top of the rest?

answer.html: boolean add(String element) { long h = hash64(element); int index = (int) (h & ((1 << p) - 1)); // low p bits pick the register long rest = (h >>> p) | (1L << (64 - p)); // the other bits, with a stop bit on top int rank = Long.numberOfTrailingZeros(rest) + 1; // zeros before the first 1, plus one if (rank <= registers[index]) return false; // a run this long was seen already registers[index] = (byte) rank; return true; }

alt.html: fun add(element: String): Boolean { val h = hash64(element) val index = (h and ((1L shl p) - 1)).toInt() // low p bits pick the register val rest = (h ushr p) or (1L shl (64 - p)) // the other bits, with a stop bit on top val rank = rest.countTrailingZeroBits() + 1 // zeros before the first 1, plus one if (rank <= registers[index]) return false // a run this long was seen already registers[index] = rank.toByte() return true }

recap: A bitmap is a string read bit by bit. If every card has a small, dense number, one bit per card per day gives exact daily counts (BITCOUNT) and combinations of days (BITOP) for 125 KB per million cards.

A HyperLogLog estimates how many different items it has seen in at most 12 KB, usually within 0.81%. Each of its 16,384 registers keeps the longest run of zero bits in the hashes that land there. It can't list or remove items, and PFMERGE gives exactly the count of several keys together.
A geo index is a sorted set whose scores are 52-bit geohashes, so nearby points get nearby scores. Distances treat the Earth as a ball, with up to 0.5% error.

Redis 8.0 ships JSON, the Bloom filter and other structures that trade exactness for memory, time series, the Query Engine and vector sets inside Redis itself. A Bloom filter's "no" is always right; its "yes" needs checking.
The limit: each structure answers one narrow question, some only roughly. Decide whether the answer must be exact before you pick one, because a HyperLogLog on a bill is off by thousands of cards.

explain.prompt: A shop owner asks why the "different cards today" number on her screen doesn't quite match the exact report the company sends her, and whether adding up the hourly numbers would fix it. Explain.
explain.answer: The screen uses a HyperLogLog, which estimates how many different cards paid in a fixed 12 KB per key instead of storing every card. It hashes each card, and in each of 16,384 registers it remembers the longest run of zero bits it has seen. That gives an estimate with a standard error of about 0.81%, so on a million cards it can be off by several thousand, up or down. The report counts every card from the payments table, so it's exact. Adding up the hourly numbers would make things worse: a card that paid in three different hours would count three times. The right way to get a day from hours is to merge the hourly HyperLogLogs, which counts each card once. If the screen must match the report card for card, we need an exact count from the payments table, and we accept what that costs.

deeper.html:
How much do the registers matter? The lab's TinyHyperLogLog, using the classic formula, gave these errors on the same card ids:

Registers 100,000 cards 1,000,000 cards
16 +66% +38%
256 -0.4% -9.1%
4,096 +0.1% -1.0%
16,384 +0.8% -0.3%

The standard error is about 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of registers: 26% for 16 registers, 6.5% for 256, 1.6% for 4,096 and 0.81% for 16,384. Single runs scatter around that, as the table shows. Redis picks 16,384 because 12 KB is small and under 1% is good enough for most screens. Since Redis 4.0, PFCOUNT uses a better formula by Otmar Ertl instead of the classic one, which had to switch to a different method for small counts and was biased in the middle range.

The sparse form stores runs of empty registers in a few bytes. Redis converts a HyperLogLog to the full form once its sparse form passes hll-sparse-max-bytes (3,000 bytes by default). Adding to a sparse HyperLogLog is slower, which is the price of its small size.

The Bloom filter numbers in this lesson come from two formulas. For n items and a false positive rate p, the best row of bits has about -n × ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 bits and uses about -log2(p) hash functions (ln and log2 are logarithms, two buttons on a scientific calculator). For a million items at 0.1%, that's about 14.4 million bits (1.8 MB) and 10 hash functions, close to the 1.9 MB the lab server reported. Redis's Bloom filters can also grow: when one fills up, BF.ADD stacks a new, larger filter on top (the Expansion rate in BF.INFO). Reserve the size you expect rather than rely on that.

A geohash's precision comes from its 52 bits: 26 for longitude and 26 for latitude. 26 bits split the latitudes Redis accepts, about 170 degrees, into cells about 0.3 m tall, which is why GEOPOS gives your point back a few centimeters off.
